messages.subject: It's Alive! San Francisco's Office Market Rises From the Dead
messages.body:

Monday, October 26, 2026

The Big Picture

Welcome to Trepp's latest offering – The CRE Rundown. Enjoy and send any questions or comments to therundown@trepp.com. Know anyone who might benefit from receiving The CRE Rundown? Send them the link here [link retained in original Gmail message]

The monster that is the San Francisco office market has been brought back to life by its very own Dr. Frankestein: artificial intelligence companies. 

AI companies accounted for 37.4% of San Francisco's office leasing activity through the first three quarters of this year, taking more than 4.4 million sf—more than double the 2.1 million sf they leased during all of 2025—according to Cushman & Wakefield.

The leasing activity has pushed the city's office availability rate down to 27.2% in the third quarter, from 33.6% a year ago and a peak of roughly 37% in 2024, according to Savills.  

San Francisco's office market, like many others, struggled in the wake of the Covid lockdowns, as remote and hybrid work reduced demand for space and prompted companies to shrink their footprints. The city recorded negative net absorption between 2020 and 2024, meaning tenants vacated more space than they occupied. Now, a new wave of AI companies is helping revive the market, with net absorption turning positive in 2025 and remaining positive through the first three quarters of 2026, according to Cushman.   

The two largest AI deals this quarter came from Sierra AI and Brex, which both renewed and expanded existing space, suggesting continued confidence in the sector's growth. Sierra AI's lease at 185 Berry St. now to totals 351,000 sf, while Brex is taking 215,374 sf at 270 Brannan St.  

As demand strengthens, competition for premium office space is intensifying, pushing rents higher. San Francisco's average asking rent rose 5.1% year over year to $70.31/sf in the third quarter, according to Savills. Although office space remains abundant, competition for premium properties is giving landlords greater pricing power. 

The City by the Bay's office market is showing signs of life, but Dr. Frankenstein's work is far from finished. With availability still above 27%, AI companies, along with tenants in other sectors, will need to keep expanding to turn the initial jolt into a lasting recovery.

The buyer lined up an $82.1 million loan from City National Bank of Florida.

One Boca Place sits on 7.75 acres at 2255 West Glades Road, just west of Interstate 95. The four-story property was built in 1986 and includes a 1,110-space parking garage. It also has a conference center, cafe, fitness center, on-site car wash, and a Regis coworking center.

The Big Picture

Welcome to Trepp's latest offering – The CRE Rundown. Enjoy and send any questions or comments to therundown@trepp.com. Know anyone who might benefit from receiving The CRE Rundown? Send them the link here [link retained in original Gmail message]

A total of $2.24 billion of securitized seniors-housing debt is scheduled to reach hard maturity between next month and December 2027.

The maturities span 156 loans, with age-restricted properties accounting for the largest share of the balance at $743.9 million, or 33.23%. Independent living accounts for another $615.2 million, or 27.48%, while $515.8 million, or 23.04%, is tied to properties with an unspecified subtype.

A total of 14.47% of the loans in the hard maturity cohort have a debt yield less than 8% and 10.39% have a debt yield less than 6%, but a large slug of the latter remains current with its payments.

Overall, 1.75% of the maturing balance is delinquent, while 1.89% is in special servicing.

A total of 19 loans with a balance of $140.2 million are scheduled to mature in the last two months of 2026. Of those loans, 47.47% carry debt yields of less than 6%. However, all of those loans are current, and none is in special servicing.

Overall, seniors-housing fundamentals appear solid, as occupancy reached 90.4% in the third quarter, up from 89.9% in the previous quarter and 88.7% a year earlier, according to the National Investment Center for Seniors Housing & Care. Demand is supported by the aging U.S. population, as more Baby Boomers—those born between 1946 and 1964—enter the age groups most likely to need senior-living services.

Assisted living has the highest delinquency rate among identified seniors-housing subtypes in the maturity cohort, with 10.16% of its $328.9 million of debt maturing through next December classified as delinquent. And 23.54% of that balance, or about $77.4 million, has a debt yield below 8%. That includes 15.05%, or about $49.5 million, that falls below 6%.

Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae account for 95.23% of the seniors-housing debt facing hard maturities through December 2027. Fannie does not report subtypes for its seniors-housing loans, so those loans are included in the unspecified category mentioned above.

A hard maturity represents a loan with no remaining contractual extension options. Borrowers must repay the debt at maturity or negotiate an alternative with the lender.

Brandywine Realty Trust has sold the Solaris, a 341-unit apartment property in Austin, Texas, for $136 million, or $398,827/unit. The buyer was not immediately known, according to the Austin Business Journal [link retained in original Gmail message]

The apartment building shares a 4.2-acre site with One Uptown, an office building that is 97% leased.

The sale is part of the Philadelphia REIT's plan to dispose of as much as $300 million of real estate this year.

➯ TruAmerica Pays $120.5Mln for Atlanta-Area Apartment Property

TruAmerica Multifamily has paid $120.5 million, or $270,179/unit, for the 446-unit Bricks at Perimeter Center apartment complex in Dunwoody, Ga.

The Los Angeles investment firm acquired the property from Clark Ventures of Atlanta in a deal brokered by CBRE.

The sale was first reported by Bisnow.

The five-story property serves as collateral for a $64.18 million loan that's securitized in FREMF, 2019-K99. The loan pays a fixed rate of 3.5% percent and matures in August 2029, according to servicer data compiled by Trepp Inc [link retained in original Gmail message]

Bricks at Perimeter was built in 2006 at 302 Perimeter Center North, about 14 miles north of downtown Atlanta. The property was 95% occupied and generated $5.77 million of net operating income through the 12-month period ending in June. That would give TruAmerica's purchase price a capitalization rate of 4.71%.

messages.subject: Credit Weekly: Rated BB, Priced Like Something Else
messages.body:
View this post on the web at [link retained in original Gmail message]

When people talk about HY repricing, they usually point to CCCs where spreads touched 1,127bps last week. This is the widest in over 3 years with most of the damage in cable and telecom. But CCCs are only 8% of the HY market and a good share of that stress sits in a few capital structures that were in trouble well before the recent selloff. The more interesting move is happening elsewhere.
You’ve probably seen the charts floating around. HY data center bonds have widened about 136bps since mid-September, far more than the index over the same period. Most of this paper is rated BB too yet currently trades ~150bps wide of the single-B index.
That is a strange place for a BB bond to sit. Either the ratings are wrong or the spread is pricing something the ratings were never designed to capture, and I think we all know which one it is. What’s more important, however, is that this paper was supposed to be the lower-risk part of a HY portfolio, and it has behaved like anything but.
In case you missed it, I published Part 1 of my CoreWeave series [ [link retained in original Gmail message] ] last week, covering the 8 biggest misconceptions about the credit. Part 2 comes out this week.
How a Lease Becomes a BB to Begin With
Most of these bonds are closer to project finance than traditional corporate credit. They typically sit in an SPV that owns a campus with one long-term lease to one tenant, and the debt is sized to the rent that lease generates. The ratings rest mainly on the lease and the tenant behind it.
Why are these rated BB to begin with? The leases typically run longer than the bonds with fixed rent escalators and the tenant carrying most of the operating costs, so the cash flow looks more like an annuity. The debt often amortizes from that rent and bondholders have security over the campus and the lease. When the tenant is a hyperscaler, the counterparty standing behind the rent is investment grade. In some deals, the tenant is a neocloud but a hyperscaler backstops the rent, which gets you most of the way there.
At the same time, plenty of things keep them from being rated higher. Many deals fund campuses that aren’t built yet, and the agencies won’t give full credit to rent that depends on a building being finished. One campus and one tenant also means no diversification inside the structure. A lot of the issuers started as bitcoin miners with short track records as data center operators and limited balance sheets to support a project that runs over budget. Where the tenant is itself sub-IG, as with CoreWeave, the rating also has to absorb the tenant’s own credit risk. And most of these bonds mature in 2030 or 2031 with a meaningful balance still outstanding, so repayment depends on the market being open when the debt comes due.
The risks that kept these deals out of IG such as construction, concentration, and the refinancing, are EXACTLY the risks the market has repriced in recent weeks. The leases themselves mostly haven’t changed. 
High Dispersion Amongst Issuers
You’d think a cohort this similar would trade together but there’s quite a bit of dispersion across issuers. Spreads run from TeraWulf at 222bps to Zenith Arc at 848bps. The whole sector has gone wider since issuance with a few exceptions (mostly early deals that came with fat new-issue premiums). A handful of factors explain most of the dispersion.
The first is who pays the rent. Someone like TeraWulf whose tenant is Fluidstack has a backstop from Google and that gets priced very differently from a lease with a neocloud like CoreWeave, where the tenant is itself a leveraged credit trading near 1,000bps. Galaxy and Core Scientific both lease to CoreWeave, and both sit at the wider end.
The second is how far along the project is. A campus that’s built, energized and collecting rent carries very different risk from a site still under construction. The further you are from completion, the more you’re underwriting execution... whether the contractor holds to budget, the equipment arrives on schedule and the power comes on when promised. With recent budgets running well above $13mm per MW, overruns are not a hypothetical.
The third is location. Power availability, interconnection timelines, local permitting and tax treatment vary a lot by state and county, and they decide whether a campus delivers on time and what it costs to run once it does.
And don’t forget structure and the parent. These issuers are project-level vehicles, and if costs run past the contingency budget, the project may need more capital from the parent. Some are sitting on excess cash, while others may have little or no access to capital at all. You get the parent’s support until the buildings are finished, and after that you’re relying on the project and the lease. These structures do amortize, so they de-risk as rent comes in and principal comes down, but the pace is different in every deal.
Small in the Index, Large in the Year’s Supply
By market value HPC is still a small slice of HY, roughly $46bn of face or ~3% of the market. Run a rough weighted-spread calc and a 136bps move in this sector accounts for only about 4bps of index-level widening, which is why the headline spread barely notices.
Across the broader data center financing category, borrowers have brought ~$37bn of new supply this year, just under 30% of all non-refinancing HY issuance.
Nearly the entire HY buyer base owns some of this paper too and most of it was bought as BB exposure, a way to pick up extra spread without stepping down into single-B operating risk. Those positions have now underperformed the rest of their BB books.
The Case That This Is Technical
Now, a good part of this could be technical. Heavy supply needs concessions to clear, crowded positioning unwinds fast when equity sentiment turns, and rising Treasury yields hit anything bought for all-in yield. The tightest names in the cohort have held up reasonably well, which tells you the market is differentiating. If budgets stabilize and campuses deliver close to schedule, some of this spread comes back.
But you have to separate three kinds of risk. First is expected credit loss... does the tenant pay, does the project finish, and what do recoveries look like if it doesn’t. Without updated project costs and delivery timelines it’s hard to say how much that has moved. Next is mark-to-market risk, meaning how far spreads can widen without any change in the contractual payments, and that’s most of what we’re seeing this fall. Lastly is refi risk, meaning what happens when a project needs more capital or has to refinance its balance in 2030 or 2031. And that one feeds right back into the first, because a wider market for this paper makes both of those harder.
Even if the move is mostly technical, look at how this paper behaves under pressure. The cohort shares similar risks so they tend to move together but the move hasn’t been even. The bonds leased to CoreWeave have widened about 150bps on average over the past month, roughly twice as much as the lower beta names. A lot of this paper bought as low-vol BB carry is trading with equity-like sensitivity to sentiment. If you’re a PM who sized this as a defensive allocation, that volatility is a problem even if recoveries end up fine.
What It Means for the Rest of the Market
The direct hit to the index is small. As I noted above, the widening in this cohort accounts for only a few basis points of the headline spread. The bigger effect is on how HY behaves. A meaningful slice of the BB bucket is now tied to AI sentiment, so moves in AI equities and neocloud credit now show up in what used to be one of the steadier parts of the market. And with BBs at a record share of HY fund holdings, a lot of portfolios are carrying more AI exposure in their BB allocation than the ratings suggest.
The bigger risk is what happens to the tenants. If debt markets keep pulling back from AI borrowers without other sources of revenue, the neoclouds that lease these campuses will find it much harder to fund themselves, and some won’t make it. That’s when tenant risk becomes a credit issue for the landlords’ bonds.

messages.subject: Outside Money
messages.body:
View this post on the web at [link retained in original Gmail message]

The Beacon · October 25, 2026
By Bob Sheehan, CFA, CMT
Executive Summary
The economy has one engine running hot. Core capital goods orders rose 14.1% year over year in August, the fastest since August 2021. Real retail sales grew 2.09%. That 12.0-point gap between business investment and the consumer is the widest since February 2012 (Census Bureau, August data, latest available).
That engine has switched from internal to outside money. Bank business loans grew 9.98% year over year in September, the fastest since March 2023 (Federal Reserve). This week Meta reported its first quarterly cash burn in more than a decade, raised its 2026 capex outlook to $135-145 billion, and set up a new class of non-voting shares to raise equity. Its five-year credit default swap hit a record 114.79 bps (Reuters, Oct. 22).
Outside money is expensive. The 10-year TIPS yield closed at 2.95% on Oct. 5, the highest since November 2008. Even after Thursday’s sharp rally it sits at 2.64% (Treasury, Oct. 22). The Federal Reserve hiked in September and futures price a 92% chance of a hold next Wednesday (CME fed funds futures, Oct. 23).
The market has started to charge for the build. On Thursday, Oct. 22, the PHLX Semiconductor Index fell 6.79%, the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.60%, and the S&P 500 closed at 7,663.43, below its 50-day average. The 10-year Treasury yield dropped 17 bps to 4.96%, mostly through the real yield.
Our read: the expansion is intact, but it now depends on a sector whose funding costs are set by markets that just repriced. Labor is low-hire, low-fire. Inflation is 3.7%. Policy is tight. We expect the market to keep sorting the builders by who can fund themselves, and we would lean against the parts of the trade that need outside money.
Data note: our database runs through Oct. 19-21 depending on the series. Weekly and daily figures after that come from the official releases cited in the text.
Highlighting the data that matters most. This is macro, illuminated
Macro Context
Two speeds
Most of the year’s macro debate has asked whether the economy is overheating or rolling over. The answer depends on which half you look at.
Business investment is booming. New orders for nondefense capital goods excluding aircraft, the Census Bureau’s core capex series, reached $87.6 billion in August. That is up 1.6% on the month and 14.1% on the year. Shipments of the same goods, the input to GDP, grew 11.3% year over year, the fastest since February 2022. Orders lead shipments, and orders are still running ahead.
The consumer is holding up but not much more. Real retail sales rose 2.26% year over year in September (Census Bureau, deflated by CPI). The University of Michigan’s preliminary October sentiment reading was 46.3, down from 48.1 in September, with current conditions at 44.7. The final October reading came in at 48.0 (current conditions 46.7, expectations 48.8; University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers, released 10 a.m. ET Oct. 23). Headline retail sales did rise 0.8% in September, but a good share of that was price: gasoline rose 9.1% on the month in the CPI.
Figure 1 is the gap that matters. When business investment grows 12 points faster than real consumer spending, the expansion has a single point of failure. In 2011 and 2012 the gap was this wide because the consumer was still repairing its balance sheet after the financial crisis. This time it is wide because one theme, artificial intelligence infrastructure, is pulling forward a decade of spending on chips, data centers, power and cooling.
That matters for how we read the rest of the data. An expansion led by capex has different sensitivities than one led by the consumer. Households in the U.S. mostly locked in their mortgage rates years ago; as we wrote in Termed Out, the rate on the stock of debt has barely moved. Capex is funded at the margin, at today’s price. That is where the economy is now exposed.
Labor: nobody leaves, nobody gets let go
The labor market has been the reason recession calls kept failing, and this week added to that. Initial jobless claims fell 6,000 to 194,000 in the week ended Oct. 17, below the 200,000 consensus. The four-week average is 197,750 (Department of Labor, Oct. 22). That is the sixth straight week at or below 200,000. The low for the year, 189,000 in July, was the lowest since 1969.
Firing is rare. Hiring is also rare. Payrolls rose 29,000 in September after 133,000 in August and a 10,000 decline in July (Bureau of Labor Statistics). The unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2% from 4.1%. The quits rate held at 1.9% in August, below the 2.0% level we treat as a pre-recession warning, and the hires rate was 3.3%.
Workers are staying put because few employers are adding headcount, and employers are not firing because they still remember how hard hiring was in 2021 and 2022. That holds the labor market together as long as revenue holds. Continuing claims rose 25,000 to 1,728,000 in the week ended Oct. 10, a small move, but it is the series that shows whether people who lose a job can find another one. Firms are holding headcount while they spend on equipment. If the capex cycle stalls, the labor market has little cushion: few open roles to absorb anyone let go, and low quits mean little natural attrition to lean on first.
Inflation: the energy shock meets a sticky core
Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August (BLS, Oct. 14). Energy was the driver: up 20.4% on the year, with gasoline up 9.1% on the month. Core CPI rose 0.3% on the month and 2.6% on the year, both a tenth above consensus. Shelter rose 0.4%.
Producer prices ran hotter. The September PPI rose 1.3% against a 0.6% consensus, with the core up 0.7% (BLS). The ISM manufacturing prices index jumped to 77.9 in September from 71.1, and the services prices index rose to 74.0 (Institute for Supply Management). The core PCE price index was up 3.0% year over year in August (Bureau of Economic Analysis).
The worry in Figure 3 is the pipeline. Pipeline prices pass through to core goods with a lag, and the ISM manufacturing gauge is at its highest since May. Oil is no help. December Brent futures rose 4.00% Thursday to $113.17, the highest since May, on reports of strikes on Iran (Reuters, Oct. 22). Households feel it: one-year inflation expectations in the preliminary Michigan survey were 4.7%, and five-to-ten-year expectations were 3.5%.
For the capex thesis, inflation matters through one channel: it keeps policy tight, and it keeps the cost of outside money high.
From cash flow to capital markets
For most of this cycle the biggest spenders paid for the build out of operating cash. That made the boom unusually insensitive to interest rates. A company funding $100 billion of data centers from free cash flow does not care much what the 10-year yield does.
That is changing, and this week made it concrete.
Meta’s third-quarter results showed capital expenditures of $34.91 billion against operating cash flow of $32.79 billion, a negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion. Reuters reported it as the company’s first cash burn in more than a decade. Management raised the low end of its 2026 capex outlook by $5 billion to a $135-145 billion range. Long-term debt is up $22.2 billion this year to $80.9 billion. There have been no buybacks in 2026. Alongside the results, the company created a new class of non-voting shares that could raise what it called “hundreds of billions” over time; the filing says the purpose is to fund investment without adding debt that could hurt its ratings. The stock fell 6.98% and the company’s five-year CDS reached a record 114.79 bps (Reuters, Oct. 22).
One of the most profitable companies in the world told the market that its own cash flow no longer covers its spending, that it would rather sell equity than borrow more, and that it is watching its rating. The credit market answered by charging more to insure its debt than at any time on record.
That is one company, and we would not build a macro call on a single earnings report. The aggregate data say the same thing.
Commercial and industrial loans on bank balance sheets reached $2,987.85 billion in the week of Oct. 7, up 10.97% over 52 weeks (Federal Reserve H.8). On a monthly basis, business loans grew 9.98% in the year to September, adding $268.4 billion. A year earlier they were shrinking 3.12%. In the July Senior Loan Officer Survey, a net 16.1% of banks reported stronger demand for C&I loans, while the net share tightening standards was 0.0. Banks are meeting the demand.
Figure 4 puts the three together: loan demand, loan growth and capex orders are all rising. Corporate America is borrowing to build.
On its face, that is good news: credit is available, banks are willing, and the investment gets done. The risk is in the terms. Debt-funded capex is rate-sensitive capex. Equity-funded capex depends on the stock price. The builders have moved from a funding source that ignored the market to two that depend on it.
Monetary Dynamics
Tight, and holding
The Federal Reserve raised the federal funds target range to 3.75%-4.00% on Sept. 16 in a 12-0 vote. The effective rate is 3.88% (New York Fed, Oct. 21). Fed funds futures price a 92% chance of a hold at the Oct. 27-28 meeting and an 8% chance of another 25 bps hike, down from about 16% a week earlier (CME fed funds futures, Oct. 23). December is where the hike debate lives now.
The odds likely came down for two reasons. Thursday’s equity selloff tightened financial conditions without the Fed having to act. And the labor data, for all their strength in claims, show a payroll trend that has slowed to a crawl. The committee can afford to wait for the October jobs report on Nov. 6 and the October CPI on Nov. 10.
Figure 5 is our read on what the market expects from policy. The 2-year Treasury yield minus the effective fed funds rate captures the path priced over the next two years. On Oct. 19 it was 89 bps (4.77% minus 3.88%). After Thursday it was 77 bps (4.65% minus 3.88%, Treasury and New York Fed). A positive spread means the market expects the funds rate to be higher on average over the next two years than it is today. With the ISM prices index at 77.9, a spread near zero would mean the market had stopped believing in further hikes despite pipeline inflation. At 77 bps, the market still leans toward more tightening, though part of that spread is term premium.
Real rates: the price of the build
The bigger story for capex is real rates. The 10-year TIPS yield started the year at 1.94%, rose to 2.68% on hike day, and reached 2.95% on Oct. 5. That was the highest close since Nov. 24, 2008. The five-year TIPS yield hit 2.73% on Sept. 28, also the highest since November 2008 (Treasury).
Figure 6 splits the 10-year yield into its two parts. Breakeven inflation has been stable; the 10-year breakeven was 2.35% on Oct. 20, and the five-year was 2.39%. Almost all of this year’s rise in nominal yields came through the real component. That is the cleanest measure of what the market charges for capital before inflation, and it is the hurdle every data center now has to clear.
Thursday’s rally lowered the level and left the picture intact. The 10-year Treasury fell 17 bps to 4.96%, its first close under 5% in nearly a month. The 10-year TIPS yield fell 12 bps to 2.64%, and the five-year TIPS yield fell 22 bps to 2.33% (Treasury, Oct. 22). Breakeven inflation barely moved. What the market priced was lower real growth and some flight to safety, which is what you would expect when the market’s main growth engine wobbles.
The term premium is also elevated. The Kim-Wright 10-year term premium was 0.9857 percentage points on Oct. 16 (Federal Reserve Board). The 2-year to 10-year curve was 38 bps positive on Oct. 19 and 31 bps after Thursday. The federal deficit for fiscal year 2026 was $1.99 trillion, up 12% (Treasury). Long-dated supply is not going away, and the builders are now competing with the Treasury for the same duration buyers.
Gold follows real yields again
In levels, gold spent 2022-2025 rising alongside higher real yields, with central bank buying swamping the usual relationship. On shorter horizons the link held, and in 2026 it has tightened. On 21-day changes, the correlation between gold and the 10-year real yield has been -0.60 since February, compared with -0.46 over 2022-2025 and -0.41 over 2005-2021 (Lighthouse calculation from Treasury and NYSE Arca data). The SPDR Gold Shares ETF closed at 378.95 on Oct. 21, 23.6% below its Jan. 29 peak of 495.90, and below both its 50-day (395.87) and 200-day (414.64) averages. Gold futures fell another 2.66% Thursday to 4,039.8.
Gold matters here as a check on our real-rate story. If investors were losing faith in the dollar or the Fed, gold would rise with real yields. Instead it is moving against them, which tells us the market reads high real rates as a policy and growth story. The broad trade-weighted dollar was 121.40 on Oct. 16 (Federal Reserve), and the ICE dollar index was 101.62 on Oct. 22.
Market Technicals
The index lost its first line
The S&P 500 closed at 7,663.43 on Oct. 22, down 1.21% on the day and 1.99% below its Oct. 6 record of 7,818.93 (S&P Dow Jones Indices). It closed below its 50-day average, which we calculate at 7,703.15 including Thursday’s close. The 200-day average sits at 7,287.80, about 4.9% below.
Breadth was mediocre going in. On Oct. 20, 55.8% of S&P 500 members traded above their 200-day averages and 53.2% above their 50-day. The McClellan Summation Index for the S&P 500 was -120.46. Those are the readings of a market that has been rotating rather than rising, which is what we described in The Fourth Rotation. Thursday the rotation turned into selling. The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished up 0.02% at 52,867.98 and the Russell 2000 up 0.11%, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.60%, its worst day since June. The Cboe Volatility Index rose 14.09% to 19.03.
What we are watching on the index: a close back above the 50-day average would put this in the same category as the three earlier rotations this year, where leadership changed hands without the index breaking. A move toward the 200-day average with breadth falling under 40% above the 200-day would tell us the market is pricing a funding problem for the whole AI complex, including the companies with the strongest cash flow.
Semis: the market is sorting the builders
The PHLX Semiconductor Index fell 6.79% on Thursday. Lam Research dropped 11.8%, CoreWeave about 10%, and GE Vernova 10.64% (Reuters, AP, Oct. 22). Consumer staples gained 3.31%, the best sector. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF closed Oct. 21 at 556.70, 16.8% below its June 22 high of 668.91 and below its 50-day average of 577.56, though still above its 200-day of 514.05.
Figure 9 puts semis against the average stock. The ratio of SMH to the equal-weight S&P 500 is 19.8% below its June 22 peak but still 3.3% above its 200-day average (Oct. 21). The real yield, inverted, sits on the same chart because the timing is close: the ratio peaked in June, and real yields made their big move from June to October.
Look at who fell hardest on Thursday. CoreWeave depends on debt markets to fund GPU purchases. GE Vernova sells power equipment to data center developers whose projects need financing. Lam sells the equipment that turns those budgets into chips. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang said this week that capital demand from the neoclouds far exceeds supply. He meant it as a sign of demand. We read it as a funding constraint.
The 200-day average on the ratio is our line. As long as semis hold above it relative to the average stock, this looks like a correction inside a leadership trend. A break below it, with real yields still above 2.5%, would mean the market has stopped paying for the build at these rates.
Credit: calm overall, priced at the margin
High-yield credit spreads were 329 bps on Oct. 19 (ICE BofA via the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis), up from a 2026 low of 260 bps on Aug. 28 but below the 346 bps high of March 30. Investment-grade spreads were 87 bps, up from 79 at the start of the year. Both sit in the lower fifth of their history since 1997. The Thursday close is not yet in our data (Oct. 22 close: high-yield 340 bps, investment-grade 89 bps; ICE BofA via the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, fetched 10:27 a.m. ET Oct. 23).
Figure 10 shows why aggregate credit stays calm. Spreads follow layoffs, and layoffs have not shown up. As long as initial claims stay near 200,000, high-yield spreads have little reason to blow out. The stress is in specific credits. As we laid out in The Beam on Thursday, the widening this autumn has come from the weakest borrowers, and now a top-rated issuer’s CDS is at a record. The market is pricing the build credit by credit, starting with the borrowers that need the most money.
We treat 300 bps on the high-yield index as the line where credit is priced for perfection, and 500 bps as the line where it is pricing a recession. The index is closer to the first. What would worry us is a move above the March high of 346 bps while claims stay low. That would mean credit is pricing a funding problem before the labor market shows one.
Crypto’s dollar base is shrinking
The combined market value of Tether and USD Coin, the two largest dollar stablecoins, was $255.16 billion on Oct. 21. That is down 1.02% over 30 days and 4.84% below the May 8 peak of $268.15 billion (DefiLlama). Bitcoin was 81,163 at 4 p.m. ET on Oct. 22, down 4.08% on the day and 34.9% below its record of 124,752.53 on Oct. 6, 2025. It is just below its 50-day average of 81,841 and above its 200-day of 72,810 (Oct. 21).
We would not overstate the link. Over short windows, the relationship between stablecoin growth and Bitcoin returns is close to zero in our data. Over longer windows it is positive but loose. What the stablecoin data tell us is narrower: the dollar liquidity that sits inside crypto has stopped growing, and it has been shrinking for five months. Those coins are backed mostly by Treasury bills. When real rates are this high, the opportunity cost of holding a zero-yield token is high too. It is one more corner of the market where high real rates are pulling money out.
Conclusion
The thread
Put the pieces together and the picture is consistent. The U.S. expansion rests on business investment growing 12 points faster than the real consumer. That investment has shifted from cash flow to outside money: bank loans growing at the fastest pace since early 2023, record corporate borrowing, and now new equity. Outside money is priced off real yields that reached their highest level since 2008 this month. The Fed is holding at a restrictive setting with headline inflation at 3.7% and pipeline prices rising.
This week the market started charging for that combination. The response was orderly: high-yield spreads near the bottom of their range, the Dow flat, and staples bid. But the selling was concentrated in the companies and suppliers that most need financing, and it came alongside the largest one-day decline in the 10-year yield since March 2023 (Dow Jones Market Data). When yields fall that fast on a growth scare, the market is telling you where it thinks the weak point is.
We are not calling the end of the capex cycle. Orders are still rising, banks are still lending, and labor is intact. Our view is that the cycle has entered a phase where funding cost matters, and that the market will sort the builders by who can fund themselves. That sorting favors balance sheets with net cash, lenders and suppliers paid up front, and the parts of the economy that do not need the capital markets this year. It works against borrowers that need to refinance or raise money at today’s real rates.
What would change our mind
We hold this view with conviction, and we will drop it if the data turn. Specifically:
Real yields fall and stay down. A 10-year TIPS yield back below 2.25% for more than a few weeks would ease the funding constraint enough to restore the self-funding story. It was 2.64% on Oct. 22.
Semis hold their relative trend. If SMH relative to the equal-weight S&P 500 holds above its 200-day average through the hyperscaler earnings season and reclaims its 50-day, the market is telling us the funding concerns are priced.
Capex orders roll over. If September core capex orders, due Monday, Oct. 26, fall sharply and the three-month trend turns negative, the binding constraint is demand, and our framing is wrong in a different direction. The three-month annualized growth rate was 16.5% through August.
Credit confirms. A high-yield spread above 346 bps with initial claims still under 220,000 would push us from “sorting” to “funding stress” and toward a broader risk-off stance.
The consumer reaccelerates. Real retail sales growth above 4% year over year would narrow the gap in Figure 1 and reduce the economy’s reliance on capex. It was 2.26% in September.
The week ahead
Next week tests every piece of this thesis. September durable goods on Monday, Oct. 26 gives us the capex read. The Conference Board’s confidence index and new home sales come Tuesday. The FOMC decision is Wednesday, Oct. 28, at 2 p.m. ET. The advance estimate of third-quarter GDP and September personal income and spending, including the PCE price index, are Thursday, Oct. 29. The Employment Cost Index is Friday, Oct. 30. Three of the largest hyperscalers report in the same stretch (Microsoft after the close and Alphabet with a 4:30 p.m. ET call on Wednesday, Oct. 28, and Amazon with a 5 p.m. ET call on Thursday, Oct. 29, per the companies’ investor relations announcements of Oct. 7, Oct. 6 and Oct. 15). The midterm elections follow on Nov. 3.
Friday’s flash PMIs from S&P Global (October flash composite 57.6, down from 58.4 in September; S&P Global, released 9:45 a.m. ET Oct. 23) and the final Michigan survey set the tone into the weekend.
Additionally, stay tuned for some surveys, announcements, & rollouts the next couple days & weeks. In the meantime, please don’t hesistaye to reach out with any comments or questions. If it’s concerns you have, these aren’t the droids you’re looking for. 👋
That’s our view from the Watch. Until next call to port, we’ll keep the light on...

messages.subject: Hiking Into a Drain
messages.body:
View this post on the web at [link retained in original Gmail message]

The Fed is tightening, Treasury is draining reserves with no buffer left, and crypto-native flows have gone quiet. 
Our Crypto Liquidity Impulse [ [link retained in original Gmail message] ]says wait; here’s what would change that.
The Fed raised rates on September 17, its first hike since July 2023, and futures now put roughly three in four odds on doing it again in December. That alone would be a headwind for anything priced off liquidity. The bigger story is quieter. Treasury has rebuilt its cash account by $122 billion over the last 13 weeks, and with the reverse repo facility down to $0.2 billion there is no buffer left to absorb it, so the money comes out of bank reserves and money funds. Repo is saying the same thing: SOFR is back at IORB after spending most of October 1 to 3 bps below it. High yield spreads are 60 bps wider in four weeks. Crypto feels this first, because it trades on the marginal dollar. Bitcoin rallied 48% off the June 30 low while liquidity was merely flat. With liquidity now draining, the bar for the next leg is higher, and we can say exactly what would clear it.
We're also bringing crypto back as a regular part of what we publish. It's a big market, it sits right where our plumbing work and our liquidity work meet, and we've been too quiet on it this year. This is the first of those pieces.
The Regime: Tightening Into a Thin Cushion
Start with policy. The target range is 3.75-4.00% after the September 17 hike, which reversed the last cut of the 2025 easing cycle (December 2025). The effective rate sits at 3.88%. CME FedWatch pricing as of October 23 puts the October 27-28 meeting at a 90-92% hold, an 8-10% chance of another 25 bps, and zero chance of a cut. December is the live meeting: about 72% odds of one more hike, and about 78.5% odds of at least one.
That is a Fed leaning against inflation that hasn't cooled. September CPI was up 3.7% on the year as reported, and our seasonally adjusted calculation from the FRED series puts it closer to 4.0%. Both are roughly double the target. The bond market has backed off a little: the 10-year sits at 4.96%, down 15 bps over four weeks and 35 bps off its October 5 high of 5.31%. Before this year, the last time the 10-year printed this high was October 2023. Ten-year breakevens are steady at 2.34%, so the yield move is coming from the real-rate side.
The balance sheet itself is a non-event, and that matters for how we read the drain. Total Fed assets are $6,754 billion, essentially unchanged over 13 weeks (+$6.2 billion). Inside that total, Treasury holdings are up $80 billion since July 1 while mortgage-backed securities are down $53 billion, consistent with MBS paydowns being rolled into Treasuries. The Fed is no longer shrinking the system in aggregate.
Treasury is doing the shrinking. The General Account is $952 billion, up $122 billion over 13 weeks and above 90% of weekly readings since 2015. In 2022 and 2023 a TGA rebuild came largely out of the reverse repo facility, which held more than $2 trillion of idle cash. That facility now holds $0.2 billion.
With nothing left in the reverse repo facility, each dollar Treasury pulls in has to come out of reserves or money funds. Net liquidity (Fed assets minus the TGA minus reverse repo) is $5,801 billion, down $116 billion over 13 weeks and $71 billion in the latest week alone. Reserves are $2.96 trillion, flat since July and about 30% below their December 2021 peak of $4.28 trillion.
Funding markets have noticed. SOFR printed 3.90% on October 22, level with IORB at 3.90%, after sitting 1 to 3 bps below it through most of October. SOFR at or above IORB isn't new this year; it happened on 80 days in 2026. It does mean the slack that opened up in early October is gone again, and banks are pricing reserves as less than abundant.
Credit is moving with it. The ICE BofA high yield spread is 340 bps, up 60 bps in four weeks and 80 bps from its 2026 tight of 260 bps on August 28. That is the widest since March 30, and wider than 86% of days over the last five years. Spreads at 340 bps aren't distressed, but the direction and speed are what feed into risk appetite.
The two pieces of good news are slow-moving. The dollar has stopped strengthening without turning into a tailwind: the DXY is 101.81, up just 0.30% over 63 trading days, and the broad trade-weighted index is up 0.73% over the same stretch. With a hawkish Fed, a weaker dollar is hard to get from here. US M2 is $23.34 trillion, growing 5.66% year over year as of August, the fastest pace since June 2022. The stock of money is growing. The flow reaching markets is shrinking.
Crypto as the Marginal-Liquidity Read
On October 21 we made the case that crypto is the cleanest available proxy for marginal global liquidity, and that stablecoin supply is the closest thing crypto has to a monetary base. The follow-up question is what that base is doing now, and how it connects to the regime above.
The answer is nothing much, which is the problem. Total USD stablecoin supply is $302.8 billion per DefiLlama. It is down $1.7 billion (0.55%) over 30 days, down $2.1 billion in the past week, and up only 0.46% over 90 days. Over a full year it has slipped 0.9%. The all-time high was $315.5 billion on May 17, so supply is about 4% below the peak. Today's 30-day growth rate ranks in the bottom 30% of readings since 2022.
This ties back to our August 2025 work in Collateral Fragility. Stablecoin issuers became a meaningful marginal buyer of T-bills, which made them procyclical: when crypto demand grows, issuers buy bills; when it stalls, that bid fades. A flat stablecoin base removes buying power from crypto, and it also takes a price-sensitive buyer out of the bill market. That happens just as Treasury is pulling cash into the TGA.
Spot bitcoin ETFs tell a similar story. US-listed funds hold about $112.5 billion. Twenty-day net flows are +$60 million, or 0.05% of assets, which is a rounding error. They were -$458 million as recently as October 20 before a +$615 million day on October 21. In February we wrote about the ETF exodus running against on-chain accumulation. The exodus has stopped; the new buyer hasn't shown up.
Leverage is clean. Perpetual funding on OKX's BTC-USDT contract is 0.49 bps per eight hours, with a seven-day average of 0.62 bps, about 6.8% annualized, and a 30-day average of 0.39 bps. That is neutral. There isn't a crowded long book waiting to be liquidated, and there isn't a short squeeze setting up either. Positioning neither adds fuel nor creates forced selling.
The CLI: Where the Signal Sits by Tier
The Crypto Liquidity Impulse is built in three tiers, each with its own lead time. The composite reading is -0.36 as of October 21, at the 34th percentile of its history since 2018. That is a second-quintile reading and an improvement on the -0.62 low of September 18.
For context: the CLI touched zero right at the low (+0.009 on July 2, -0.004 on July 1), with bitcoin's closing low at $58,559 on June 30. From there bitcoin ran 48% to $86,603 on September 21. Since August 1, the CLI has been in its bottom two quintiles on about 90% of days. The two breaks were a handful of days in late August and October 3-6.
Tier 1, the macro tide (11-13 week lead): neutral. M2 growth is accelerating and the dollar has stopped strengthening. This is the supportive tier, and given its lead time it points to late December through January. One caveat: we're using US M2 as a proxy here because a clean global M2 aggregate wasn't available for this update.
Tier 2, the plumbing (1-6 week lead): negative, and the driver. Net liquidity is down $116 billion over 13 weeks, SOFR is at IORB, and high yield is 60 bps wider in four weeks. Each component points the same way.
Tier 3, crypto-native flows (0-2 week lead): neutral to negative. Stablecoin supply is contracting slightly and ETF flows are flat. Nothing new is coming in.
Overlay, leverage: neutral. Funding near 6.8% annualized gives no signal in either direction.
The read is a split: a supportive slow tier and a negative fast tier. Historically, the fast tiers decide the next six weeks and the slow tier decides the quarter after that.
Technicals
Liquidity tells us whether the current is with us. Price structure tells us whether the market agrees. For money already holding long, we’re not panicking or rushing to sell. Our rules for entries, however, keep us from putting new money to work here. It’s a combination of a dozen measures, but to really dumb it down there’s a lot of air between the price and the 200d below. We’d want to see it reclaim those shorter-term averages or wait for it to correct nearer the gently rising 200d before dedicating more capital.
Bitcoin is $80,531, 29.7% below its 52-week high. The long-term structure is intact: price is comfortably above the 200-day and the long-term 200-week, and both are rising. The short-term structure has cracked. Price is below the 50-day, one-month momentum is negative, and bitcoin is lagging the rest of crypto. Close to the line is still on the wrong side of it.
What Would Change Our Mind
We'd rather name the conditions in advance than argue with the tape after the fact. These are the triggers that would turn the read constructive:
Treasury stops refilling. The TGA is flat or lower over four weeks, or the four-week change in net liquidity turns positive and holds for two consecutive weekly prints.
Funding loosens. SOFR moves back to 2 bps or more below IORB, or the Fed signals reserve-management bill purchases.
Credit reverses. High yield spreads go back under 300 bps, retracing most of the 80 bps widening since August.
The monetary base grows again. Stablecoin 30-day growth goes above +1%, roughly +$3 billion at today's base.
The ETF bid returns. Twenty-day ETF flows go above 0.5% of assets, roughly $560 million at today's $112.5 billion.
The signals confirm. The CLI moves back above zero and the technical picture improves. The shortest path is a close back above the 20- and 50-day (about $82,500) with one-month momentum turning positive.
And the bear-side falsifier, which would move us from waiting to defending:
Bitcoin loses the 200-day (about $72,900) while high yield keeps widening.
The FOMC on October 27-28 is the near-term wildcard. A hold is priced at 90-92%. A surprise hike, or a statement that leans firmly into December, would hit the one tier that's currently helping, by way of the dollar.
Positioning: Conditions
We frame this as conditions under our own rules, with no trade call attached:
No new entry while neither the Technicals nor the CLI clear our rules.
Existing exposure stays long for the time being as we wait and see
Selling happens only against written triggers, never because of a headline.
Conclusion
The stock of money is growing at its fastest pace since 2022, and on an 11-13 week lag that is supportive into year end. The flow is going the other way. Treasury is draining reserves with no reverse repo cushion, the Fed is hiking into 4% inflation, credit is widening, and the crypto-native channels have gone flat. Bitcoin ran 48% the last time the CLI sat near zero. It sits at -0.36 today, with price just on the wrong side of the tracks. If the plumbing heals before the tide turns, this setup improves quickly, and the list above is how we'll know.
That’s our view from the Watch. Until next call to port, we’ll keep the light on...
Bob Sheehan, CFA, CMT
Founder & Chief Investment Officer, Lighthouse Macro

messages.subject: Foundations: The Fate of the S&P 500’s Worst Stocks, the Y2K Analogue, and Time for Small Caps?
messages.body:
View this post on the web at [link retained in original Gmail message]

An astute subscriber suggested I look at the truly busted stocks through the S&P 500 breadth lens since those truly busted stocks seem to be in my wheelhouse these days.
Makes perfect sense.
To recap, in last week’s article, I looked at bear markets over the last forty years and analyzed the composition of the record highs reached by the S&P 500 index just before those bear markets began.
That article finished off with this Bear Market Heroes slide, which suggested that if this is 2000 all over again, today’s broken stocks, down more than 20% off their own highs at the recent October 6th, 2026 S&P 500 Index high, could be a decent haven through the bear market, even if it lasts years.
Of course, “down more than 20%” leaves some real estate inadequately explored, the existence of which just about every value investor is rather painfully aware.
The subscriber was right to kick some extra curiosity into me.
Never allow me any rest on my laurels!
A Potentially Rich Vein Emerges
So I took the same data, and broke the Broken into two sets - the merely Broken, down 20-40%, and the truly Busted, down more than 40% at the October 6th S&P 500 record high.
The new table is similar. As of the October 6th record day, the members of the S&P 500 are sorted into Leaders, within 10% of their 10-year highs, the Broken 20-40% off their tops, and now the Busted, off more than 40%.
The same is done for the S&P 500 as it stood, repeatedly over the last 4 decades, at record highs set on the precipice of bear markets and near-bear markets.
